1:
The title says the psalm was written when David changed his behaviour before Abimelech, who drove him away. Clarke settles the name first: the man in the history is Achish, king of Gath, called Abimelech here because that was a standing title of the Philistine kings, and no manuscript or version reads Achish in the inscription. Calvin makes the same point, comparing Pharaoh among the Egyptians and Caesar among the Romans, and recalling that the kings of Gerar in Abraham's time bore the name already. Delitzsch places the psalm among the eight assigned by their inscriptions to the persecution by Saul, composed on the weary road from Gibeah to Ziklag.

What David actually did, and whether it can be defended, divides them sharply. Henry will not justify it: it ill became an honest man to feign himself what he was not, and a man of honour to feign himself a fool. Yet he wonders at the composure of a spirit that could compose so calm a psalm in that fright, and warns against mimicking in sport those of weaker understanding, since God might have made their case ours. Calvin is harder still. The deliverance was God's work, but the intermediate sin is on no account to be excused; it would be a superfluous task to try to exculpate David, who exposed himself and the grace of the Spirit to the derision of the ungodly, and there appears in the deception some token of infirmity. He also refuses the inference that the Spirit who dictated the psalm suggested the stratagem, comparing Rebekah's subtlety over the blessing. Clarke takes a different road out. He prefers the account of the Greek, which makes David fall into an epileptic fit, froth at the mouth and fall against the doorposts, so that Achish dismissed him as a man whose mind was gone. This, he says, saves David's character; and if it cannot be vindicated in that way, then let it fall under reproach, for hypocrisy and falsehood can never be right in God's sight, whatever men ingeniously say to excuse them.

The psalm is the second acrostic, every verse beginning with a consecutive Hebrew letter, and it is defective. Clarke observes that the verse beginning with vau, which should stand between the fifth and sixth, is wholly wanting, and that the last verse stands entirely outside the series. His proposal is that the last verse originally began with the missing letter, as more than a hundred of Kennicott's manuscripts read it, and belongs after the fifth; he prints the verses in that order to show how well the connection runs. Delitzsch treats the closing verse instead as a supernumerary letter deliberately repeated, matching the device at the end of an earlier psalm, whose answering verse begins with the same word.

On the opening resolve the tone lifts. Gill takes blessing at all times to cover both the God of providence, for mercies renewed every morning, and the God of grace, for blessings irreversible and without repentance; the saints have reason to bless him in adversity as well as prosperity, since it might have been worse. Henry hears three resolutions: to praise constantly, openly, and heartily, and remarks that if we hope to spend eternity in praising God it is fit we should spend much of our time here at the work. Spurgeon presses the personal determination — he is resolved and fixed, let others do as they may — and turns the occasion into the argument: even when a mercy reminds us of our own sin with regard to it, we are not to rob God of his honour because conscience justly censures our share in the transaction. Though the hook was rusty, God sent the fish. Augustine reads the whole title allegorically instead, of a change of countenance in the priesthood and a sacrifice after the order of Melchizedek.
2:
The boast of the second verse is at once distinguished from the wrong kind. Gill makes it soul boasting and not tongue boasting, directed not to men or works of righteousness but to the Lord alone. Clarke reads it as setting oneself to praise and reckoning that the chief work. Wesley reduces it to a sentence: glorying in having so powerful and so gracious a master. Who the humble are is settled by the Hebrew. Clarke gives the afflicted, such as David had been; Ellicott says the word means those who have learnt patience in the school of suffering, and notes that the Greek and Latin render it the meek; Wesley simply says the righteous. On magnifying, Gill enters the necessary caveat — God cannot be made great by men, only declared as great as he is, and that imperfectly — while Clarke translates it as making greatness to Jehovah, showing how glorious his name is. Wesley catches the practical difficulty in doing it together: not together in place, for David was banished from the place of public worship, but in affection, so that the praises meet in the ears of the all-hearing God.

David's own case is then generalised. Gill notes that he did not seek the Lord publicly in the sanctuary, being at Gath, but mentally and silently, and that God answered groans which could not be uttered. Clarke ties it to the history, where David laid up the words of Achish's servants in his heart and was greatly afraid. Spurgeon grants the awkwardness rather than hiding it: the prayer must have been confused and full of self-sufficiency, or David would not have resorted to methods of such dubious morality; yet the limping prayer was accepted, which is the more reason to celebrate the mercy. Delitzsch marks the change of verb, the seeking here being the intense longing kind rather than the mere search.

The lightened faces are read two ways. Gill takes the sense of enlightening, following the Targum's their faces were enlightened, and adds that they must have had light before they could look, but gained more by looking; he also reports the alternative that the word means flowing, which would describe the numbers streaming to God and the swiftness of their motion. Ellicott makes the flowing primary and the shining derived from it in Aramaic, and quotes an ancient comment that he who approaches God receives the rays of intellectual light; he thinks of the dying Stephen. Wesley keeps it plain: comforted and encouraged, and not disappointed of their hope.

The encamping angel raises the largest question of the section. Gill offers either the uncreated Angel of the covenant, whose salvation is as walls and bulwarks, or a created angel, since one was enough to destroy a whole army. Wesley says flatly that the singular is put for the plural. Clarke will have neither, preferring a watchman going his rounds, with those who fear the Lord as the objects of his special care. Ellicott lists four senses the phrase bears elsewhere and concludes the psalmist uses it generally for the divine manifestation of protection, which avoids the awkward picture of one angel encamped round a single sufferer. Delitzsch holds the One, the medium of God's intercourse with the patriarchs, accompanied by inferior ministering angels, and hears an allusion to the angel-camp that joined Jacob's. Henry keeps the comfort without settling the number: the holy angels do us more good offices every day than we are aware of. On tasting, Clarke makes the promises the grand test of revelation, so that any man may know whether the religion of the Bible is true by pleading them; Spurgeon says you cannot see except by tasting; Gill spreads the goodness across the three Persons; and Clarke's old Psalter, at the young lions, reads the rich had need and they hungered.
11:
The psalm turns didactic here, and the readers notice the turn. Delitzsch marks the end of the first main division and the start of a second in a didactic tone, and settles who the children are: not children in years or in understanding, but a tender form of address from a master experienced in the ways of God, as in the opening of Proverbs. Ellicott calls it simply a common proverbial style. Gill spreads the possibilities wider — David's own family, or his subjects, to whom a king stands as father, or young people generally, or the children of God at large, particularly the least among them, who are little in their own eyes and most forward to receive instruction; the word come, he adds, means readiness to hear, not motion.

Henry and Spurgeon both dwell on the dignity of the work. Henry observes that David, a man of war anointed to be king, with his head full of cares, did not think it below him to find time for children; it does not appear he had any of his own old enough to be taught. Those in years would not be taught by him when he offered, but the tender branches are more easily bent — and it is as great a charity to put children to school whose parents neglect to teach them as to feed children whose parents have no bread. Spurgeon guesses at the occasion: perhaps the boys and girls of Gath had made sport of David in his seeming madness, and he now aims to undo the mischief by teaching. He draws lessons in the art of teaching from the word come — be winning, not repelling with harsh terms, and get them away from toys and sports, since we cannot teach them while their minds are full of other things. Henry makes the same contrast in the subject matter: David offers to teach not the harp, nor the sword and bow, nor the maxims of state policy, but the fear of the Lord, better than all arts and sciences.

Clarke uses the verse to attack a fashion in education. He prints his old Psalter's paraphrase, which promises to teach not the fables of poets nor the stories of tyrants but the dread of the Lord, and takes it as a rebuke to teaching the young heathen mythology before one sound lesson of true divinity, till their minds are imbued with it and the conduct of gods and heroes becomes their model.

What kind of life is on offer divides them. Gill runs through natural life, healthful life, prosperous life, then a spiritual life free from the remorses of a guilty conscience and the bondage of the law, and thinks eternal life may be best of all. Wesley combines them: a long and happy life begun in this world and continued for ever in the next. Ellicott keeps it earthly and literary, rendering it the man delighting in life and calling these gnomic sayings echoes from Proverbs. Henry presses hardest for the further reference, since man's life on earth consists of few days and those full of trouble; the question, he says, implies that some do ask it, though most ask who will show us any good. On the directions themselves the agreement is complete. Gill lists what the tongue must be kept from — evil speaking of God, of men, filthy and lying speech — and holds that where it is indulged the fear of God cannot be in that man. Wesley adds injurious and deceitful speeches. Ellicott warns that negative goodness is not sufficient and practical good must be added; Wesley says peace is not only to be embraced gladly when offered but followed hard after when it seems to flee. Henry suspects a backward glance in the warning to speak no guile, since those who truly repent warn others against doing likewise.
15:
The two faces of God are set against each other. Gill takes the eye upon the righteous to be more than providence — an eye of love, looking on them as clothed with the righteousness of his Son, and never withdrawn. Spurgeon presses the intentness: he watches each one as carefully as if there were only that one creature in the universe, and his ears catch the cry as a mother catches the note of a sick child, broken, plaintive and unbelieving though it be. Ellicott notes that the verse is quoted in the first epistle of Peter, and how deep a hold this psalm had on the national mind. On the contrary face, Gill is careful whom it threatens: not everyone who sins, since the righteous are not without sin, but those who live in a settled course of wickedness. Spurgeon makes it deliberate opposition — God sets himself with all his might to overthrow them. Wesley reduces both faces to a phrase: this one is his anger showing itself, and nigh means ready to hear and succour.

Ellicott finds the acrostic disturbed here as well as at the missing letter. The sense, he says, certainly requires the sixteenth verse and the fifteenth to change places, which would put one Hebrew letter before another out of order; but since the same sequence occurs in Lamentations, he concludes the order of these two letters was not invariably fixed. Clarke reports a smaller defect in the next verse, where the word righteous is absent from the Hebrew though every version preserves it, and supposes it was lost through its likeness to the verb they cry. Delitzsch, at the same place, observes that once the alphabet has been gone through a second supernumerary letter follows, and notes the deliberate interchange of prepositions between the two verses, one of gracious inclination and the other of hostile intention.

The broken heart draws the strongest writing. Gill takes the breaking to be either affliction or the sense of sin, and says God does not pass by such, but pours in oil and wine and comes to dwell with them. Clarke goes to the metal-working image behind both Hebrew words: the heart broken to shivers and the spirit beaten out, so that the hammer is necessarily implied, which recalls the word that is like a hammer breaking the rock in pieces. These two, he says, are the essential characteristics of true repentance.

The last promises are pressed hardest on the question who is meant. Gill takes the many afflictions of the righteous first of Christ, since the singular is used here where the plural was used throughout before, and his afflictions of body and soul were many though none were for sins of his own; then of every righteous man. Clarke reads it as military honour: no commander would do justice to a brave soldier by keeping him from the hottest of the battle, and the righteous are God's soldiers, suffered to be tried so that the power of grace may be shown. On the unbroken bones Gill again prefers Christ, since the bones of many martyrs were broken on the rack and wheel, and reading it of believers generally might distress anyone who suffers such an accident; Clarke keeps it general and light — God takes care of his life, and if he has scars they are honourable ones. Ellicott points to the fulfilment recorded in John. At the close, Gill takes the redemption of the soul for the continual application of what was purchased, in forgiveness and sanctification, while Clarke reads the last word not as desolate but as guilty, so that the servants shall be preserved from sin and forfeit neither life nor soul; Ellicott notes that the closing verse begins, out of its place, with the same letter and the same word as the close of an earlier psalm.
